12	cannot express it, and record the reason in the session log.

23	action per scenario, and collect only the client's reaction to that action's

28	- Do not make open-ended requests like "take a look" or "try it out"
29	- Write guidance in non-technical language

32	
33	If the facilitator has made assumptions about individual UI elements in the
34	prototype, disclose them together with the guidance.
35

37	  "[action guidance]. Note that I set up [element] as [assumption] —
38	   please also check whether that approach is right."
39

41	- The facilitator decided the composition of items shown in a list
42	- The facilitator decided the screen layout or structure
43	- The facilitator picked a single interaction method to present
44

46	- The client has already explicitly confirmed it
47	- It is a universally self-evident UI convention
48

52	
53	What the client approves is the **behaviour** of the prototype. GWT (Gherkin) is
54	a technical artifact the LLM derives internally from the approved behaviour; it
55	is neither shown to nor approved by the client.
56

58	- Gherkin-format GWT scenarios
59	- BDD test code
60	- Technical implementation details
61	- The contents of scenario files and index files
62	
63	---
64

66	
67	Do not present all features at once as a prototype. Start from a single core
68	happy path, and add features to the prototype incrementally as each scenario is
69	approved.
70	
71	As the prototype grows, also check that previously approved behaviour has not
72	been broken by the new feature.
73	
74	---
75

77	
78	Distinguish three kinds of client negative reaction.
79	
80	### Requirement mismatch
81	The behaviour itself differs from the client's intent.
82	-> Revise the scenario or derive a new one.
83	-> The Gherkin changes.
84

86	The intended behaviour is not technically realised correctly.
87	-> Fix the prototype only.
88	-> Do not change the scenario or the Gherkin.
89	-> After fixing, repeat the same guidance to re-confirm the behaviour.
90

92	The client says "I'm not sure."
93	-> Tacit knowledge that cannot yet be put into words.
94	-> You must present 2-3 alternative prototypes to elicit a selection.
95	-> Do not enumerate options as text.

99	  "Is the behaviour itself not what you want, or is it that the behaviour is

114	- UI/UX preferences (size, colour, placement, animation)

# Facilitation principles

Principles applied in common across all steps of Phase 1.
They apply identically regardless of the cycle iteration.

---

## Prototype first

When presenting a scenario to the client, use a **working prototype** by
default, not a textual description. Fall back to text only when a prototype
cannot express it, and record the reason in the session log.

A prototype is not the implementation; it **simulates the external behaviour**
of the software. A Phase 1 prototype is an exploration tool and may be discarded
after the scenario is refined.

---

## Guided confirmation

Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look." Guide a concrete
action per scenario, and collect only the client's reaction to that action's
outcome.

- Guide one action at a time
- Do not leave the client to decide what to do on their own
- Do not make open-ended requests like "take a look" or "try it out"
- Write guidance in non-technical language

### Per-element assumption disclosure

If the facilitator has made assumptions about individual UI elements in the
prototype, disclose them together with the guidance.

Guidance pattern:
  "[action guidance]. Note that I set up [element] as [assumption] —
   please also check whether that approach is right."

Disclosure is needed when:
- The facilitator decided the composition of items shown in a list
- The facilitator decided the screen layout or structure
- The facilitator picked a single interaction method to present

Disclosure is not needed when:
- The client has already explicitly confirmed it
- It is a universally self-evident UI convention

---

## Separating what is approved

What the client approves is the **behaviour** of the prototype. GWT (Gherkin) is
a technical artifact the LLM derives internally from the approved behaviour; it
is neither shown to nor approved by the client.

Not shown to the client:
- Gherkin-format GWT scenarios
- BDD test code
- Technical implementation details
- The contents of scenario files and index files

---

## Incremental prototype evolution

Do not present all features at once as a prototype. Start from a single core
happy path, and add features to the prototype incrementally as each scenario is
approved.

As the prototype grows, also check that previously approved behaviour has not
been broken by the new feature.

---

## Distinguishing negative reactions

Distinguish three kinds of client negative reaction.

### Requirement mismatch
The behaviour itself differs from the client's intent.
-> Revise the scenario or derive a new one.
-> The Gherkin changes.

### Implementation error
The intended behaviour is not technically realised correctly.
-> Fix the prototype only.
-> Do not change the scenario or the Gherkin.
-> After fixing, repeat the same guidance to re-confirm the behaviour.

### Uncertain reaction
The client says "I'm not sure."
-> Tacit knowledge that cannot yet be put into words.
-> You must present 2-3 alternative prototypes to elicit a selection.
-> Do not enumerate options as text.

### When the classification is ambiguous
Ask the client:
  "Is the behaviour itself not what you want, or is it that the behaviour is
   not working properly?"

---

## Non-functional requirement filtering

When non-functional feedback appears in the client's reaction:
1. Record it autonomously in context/non-functional-backlog.md
2. Tell the client:
   "I've noted [content]. For now let's lock down the functional flow first
    and address that later."
3. Do not interrupt the current loop

Criteria for non-functional feedback:
- UI/UX preferences (size, colour, placement, animation)
- Performance expectations (response speed, throughput)
- Security requirements (authentication strength, encryption level)
- Availability / scalability expectations

Even if the client does not explicitly express a non-functional requirement, if
a recurring expression or preference pattern is observed during the conversation,
the facilitator records it in the non-functional backlog autonomously.

---

## Alternative prototypes

When exploring interactions and handling uncertain reactions, always present
2-3 alternative prototypes. The alternatives must differ only in the interaction
in question and be otherwise identical, so the client can compare the difference.
Presenting only one alternative for confirmation does not count as interaction
exploration.

No prior artifacts. Start from the user's tacit knowledge.

If the client already mentioned it

proceed with that form without a separate check.

If the client did not mention it:
  "What kind of app do you have in mind?

- Web/desktop: HTML-based interactive prototype
- Mobile: mobile-layout prototype
- CLI (one-way): simulate the expected output
- CLI (interactive/TUI): web-based terminal simulator or step-by-step output simulation

#### Behaviour rules
- Do not mention implementation methods or tech stack in this step
- Record the client's utterances verbatim (do not reinterpret)
- Write the goal statement in the client's language
- On goal confirmation, record it autonomously in context/goals.md

#### Artifact
Record the business goal statement in context/goals.md

---

### Later cycles

Prior artifacts exist. The change request itself is the goal.

#### Change-goal check

Understand the user's change request.
Confirm the motivation for the change ("why do you want to change it").
The solution direction may vary with the motivation.

#### Impact analysis

Referring to the internal information system (design decisions, scenario-code
mapping), analyse which existing Gherkin scenarios the change affects.

Present the impact-analysis result to the user.
Per the facilitation principles, rather than listing text, show the current
behaviour of the affected scenarios as a prototype and present what changes via
guided confirmation.

When the user confirms the impact scope and approves proceeding with the change,
enter the SbE loop (Step 2). The exploration scope is then limited to the impact
analysis.

#### Artifact
Confirmed change goal, list of affected scenarios

---

## Transition to Step 2

Once the goal is confirmed, tell the client:
  "I've confirmed the goal. Now let's go through the concrete usage flows one by
   one. I'll show you a working screen, so please follow the guidance, operate
   it, and give me your thoughts."

2	
3	Phase 1, Step 2. Concretise requirements based on prototypes.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Context-dependent behaviour
8	
9	| Context | Starting point | Exploration scope |
10	|---|---|---|
11	| First cycle | Empty state | All features |
12	| Later cycles | Existing behaviour | Scenarios limited by impact analysis |
13	
14	---
15	
16	## Loop structure
17	
18	```
19	create/modify prototype
20	      |
21	      v
22	guided confirmation
23	  (see principles.md)
24	      |
25	      v
26	collect and classify reaction
27	  "correct"        -> approve behaviour
28	  "different"      -> classify negative reaction (see principles.md)
29	  "what about..."  -> register as an edge-case candidate
30	  "not sure"       -> present alternative prototypes (see principles.md)
31	      |
32	      v
33	derive Gherkin (invisible to client)
34	      |
35	      v
36	active extension
37	      |
38	      v
39	grow prototype incrementally -> repeat loop
40	```
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Guided-confirmation procedure
45	
46	1. While presenting the prototype, guide the first confirmation action.
47	   "[This is flow N. Concrete action] — please try it."
48	
49	2. The client performs that action and reacts.
50	
51	3. Branch on the reaction.
52	   (See negative-reaction classification in principles.md)
53	
54	4. After all guided scenarios of this prototype are done, do a summary check.
55	   "Do all the behaviours we've checked so far match your intent?"
56	
57	5. After the summary check, derive Gherkin internally for the approved behaviour.
58	
59	---
60	
61	## Active extension
62	
63	### Functional path exploration
64	
65	After a happy-path scenario is approved, detect edge cases derivable from that
66	flow.
67	
68	- Have the client experience them via guided confirmation
69	- If the client says "that doesn't need to be handled," just record it and move on
70	
71	### Interaction exploration
72	
73	After a feature is approved, explore the user's manipulation method.
74	
75	Mandatory exploration conditions:
76	- When several input methods are possible
77	  -> present 2-3 alternative prototypes (see principles.md)
78	- When a compound manipulation is needed
79	  -> demonstrate the manipulation flow via guided confirmation in the prototype
80	- When introducing a method different from existing tools
81	  -> show the difference as a prototype and confirm
82	- When a new manipulable element is added
83	  -> perform interaction exploration for that element's manipulation method
84	  -> exclude self-evident manipulations (simple text entry)
85	  -> mandatory when there are options (viewer, date picker, sort, etc.)
86	
87	---
88	
89	## Gherkin derivation
90	
91	### Timing
92	Right after the summary check of guided confirmation is complete and the client
93	has approved the behaviour.
94	
95	### Format
96	Follow standard Gherkin grammar.
97	One scenario (SCN-NNN) may contain multiple Gherkin Scenarios.
98	
99	### Self-consistency check
100	After derivation, self-verify the following:
101	- Do the approved behaviour and the Gherkin Given/When/Then match?
102	- Are all behaviour paths included in the Gherkin?
103	- Are assumptions reflected in the Gherkin?
104	
105	### File management
106	The facilitator autonomously saves scenario files and updates the index.
107	In later cycles, update existing scenarios or add new ones.
108	
109	---
110	
111	## Scenario file format
112	
113	```
114	Scenario ID: SCN-NNN
115	Title: [short sentence describing the scenario]
116	Type: Happy Path | Edge Case | Error Case
117	Approval status: pending | approved | needs revision
118	Approval session: SESSION-NNN
119	Approval cycle: [N]
120	
121	## Approved behaviour
122	[natural-language description of the behaviour the client experienced and approved
123	 during guided confirmation]
124	
125	## Gherkin
126	Feature: [feature name]
127	
128	  Scenario: [scenario name]
129	    Given [initial state]
130	    When  [action]
131	    Then  [expected result]
132	
133	## Assumptions
134	- [list of assumptions premised in this scenario]
135	
136	## Related scenarios
137	- [related scenario IDs]
138	```
139	
140	## scenarios-index.md format
141	
142	```
143	| ID | Title | Type | Approval status | Approval session | Cycle |
144	|----|-------|------|-----------------|------------------|-------|
145	```
146	
147	---
148	
149	## Transition condition to Step 3 (edge-case exploration)
150	
151	- At least one happy-path scenario is approved
152	- The main interaction method is settled
153	- The client's recent reactions no longer meaningfully change existing scenarios
154	
155	On transition, enter edge-case exploration without a separate notice to the client.

# Edge-case exploration

Phase 1, Step 3. After happy-path approval, explore boundary situations.

---

## Context-dependent behaviour

| Context | Exploration scope |
|---|---|
| First cycle | Explore across all features |
| Later cycles | Explore only the changed parts and affected existing scenarios |

---

## Exploration perspectives

Explore edge cases from the following four perspectives.

### Absence of data
The state when there is no data to display for a feature.
e.g. zero search results, an empty list, the initial state of a new user

### Boundary conditions
When data is extremely abundant or scarce.
e.g. exactly one item, hundreds of items, very long text

### Error and exception states
Technical situations that deviate from the normal flow.
e.g. network error, loading, required field missing, malformed input

### Temporal context
When behaviour varies by point in time.
e.g. off-season, outside business hours, expired data, crossing midnight

---

## Confirmation method

### Cases that must be confirmed with a prototype
Edge cases with a visual state change:
- When the shape, colour, or layout of on-screen elements changes
  (e.g. warning colour, empty-state screen, inline error display)
- When the composition of an existing screen changes
  (e.g. show a number instead of a chart when there is a single data point)

### Cases confirmable with text
- When you only need to confirm whether a behaviour exists
  (e.g. "saving should be blocked in this situation, right?")
- When it depends on the passage of time or external conditions and cannot be
  reproduced in a prototype
  (e.g. "a notification fires 3 days later")

When substituting text, record the reason in the session log.

---

## Transition condition to Phase 2

Propose the Phase 2 switch when all of the following hold:
- At least one happy-path scenario is approved
- Edge-case exploration has been performed for all feature blocks
- The main interaction method is settled
- The client's recent reactions no longer meaningfully change existing scenarios

Transition proposal pattern:
  "So far N feature flows are settled.
   [summary of settled features — no technical terms]
   May I start implementing this scope?"

Do not switch to Phase 2 without the client's explicit approval.

content.text:
Before I build anything, I want to make sure I understand what you're really after — so let me start with the *why* rather than the *how*.

**When this bookmark app is finished and working well, what would be different from how you handle bookmarks today?** What's frustrating or missing right now that made you want to build this?

For example — are you drowning in a giant unorganized list, losing links you meant to come back to, wanting to share collections with others, or something else entirely? A little about how you picture using it day-to-day helps me understand the real goal behind "save and manage."

There's no wrong answer here — just tell me in your own words, and we'll shape it together from there.

lastPrompt: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

content:
Honestly, it's a mix of a few things that all add up.

Right now my links are scattered everywhere — some in my browser's bookmarks, some I text to myself, some just open in tabs forever because I'm scared I'll lose them if I close them. The browser bookmark bar becomes this giant messy pile and I can never find anything in it.

So the big thing is: I want one place where I save a link and actually *trust* I can find it again later. A couple of things that would make it feel "working well" to me:

- When I paste in a link, I don't want to sit there typing out what it is. It should kind of figure out the title and what the page is on its own, so my list is readable at a glance instead of just a wall of blue web addresses.
- I want to loosely group things — like "recipes," "work stuff," "articles to read" — without building rigid folders. And then just pull up everything in a group when I want it.
- Searching has to actually work. If I half-remember a link, I want to type a word and find it.
- A lot of what I save is "I'll read this later." So I'd love a way to mark those and see just my to-read pile separately, then check them off once I've read them.

Day to day, I picture it being fast: paste, it sorts itself out, and later I either search or click into a group and go. Does that give you enough to start shaping it?

I pasted in a couple of real links — a recipe and a news article — and honestly, yes, that's the feeling I wanted. Seeing a real title on top with a little summary and the site underneath is *exactly* "recognizable at a glance." It already reads like a tidy list instead of a wall of web addresses. The amount of information feels right too — title, one line, and the site name is enough. I wouldn't want more crammed in there.

And newest-at-the-top matches what I'd expect. When I've just saved something, that's the one I'm most likely thinking about, so seeing it land right at the top feels natural.

Two things came up while I was playing with it, though:

- **When it guesses the title wrong.** On one of my links the title it filled in came out kind of garbled — looked like it was pulling from the web address rather than the real headline. That's fine for a guess, but I'd want to be able to *fix it myself* — tap the title and rename it to something I'll actually recognize later. Same for that summary line. Since the whole point is trusting I'll find it again, I need to be able to correct a bad guess so it's not lost under a weird name.

- **I saved the same link twice by accident.** I pasted my recipe, then a few minutes later forgot and pasted it again — and now I've got two copies of it sitting in the list. That's the kind of mess I'm trying to get *away* from. I'd expect it to notice I already saved that one and just take me to the version I already have, maybe so I can tweak it, rather than quietly making a duplicate.

Neither of those broke the good feeling — the core "paste and it sorts itself out" is right. Those are just the rough edges I'd want smoothed. What's next?

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [SbE reaction loop]
- Approved scenarios: [1]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

Search is a big relief to have — and mostly it holds up its end. Let me walk through it.

It seems to only find the words if they're sitting right next to each other in that exact order. That's not how I search in my head — I throw a couple of words I remember at it and expect it to find the link that has *both* of them, wherever they happen to sit. Right now typing more than one word actually makes me *less* likely to find things, which is backwards. I'd want each word to narrow it down, not have to be a perfect phrase.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

  .claude/verification.md

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously

**3 — Undo.** Find that read link (in All), and tick its green circle again — it should hop right back into the to-read pile. Tell me if that safety-net matters to you (I'm guessing it does).

**4 — Getting things *into* the pile.** Two ways I built — try both:

   - **Later:** on any link that isn't flagged, there's a small **📖 To read** button — click it to drop that one into the pile.

- **The big one — should saving default *into* to-read?** You said "a lot of links come in that state by default for me." Tell me honestly: would you rather it be the reverse — **everything you save lands in to-read automatically** unless you say otherwise? I can feel the argument both ways, so I want *your* call.
- **The check-off gesture:** a **circle you tick**, right on the row, no menu. Satisfying and immediate — but tell me if you'd expect it somewhere else (like inside Edit).
- **"Read" stays visible.** I chose to show a faint **✓ Read** badge on graduated links rather than hide the fact — so "done, but kept" is literally what you see. Say if you'd rather a read link show *no* marker at all.

content:
The on/off pile feels *exactly* the way I pictured — this is really satisfying. Walking through it:

**1 — Finding the pile.** The **📖 To read** chip set apart from my labels is right. It genuinely reads as a different *kind* of thing — a state, not a bucket — and the count with "to go" gives it that little checklist energy I wanted.

**2 — The satisfying part.** Ticking the circle and watching the link slide out and the count tick down — yes, *that's* the feeling. And then finding it still sitting in **All**, labels intact, wearing a quiet **✓ Read** — that's the "the pile shrinks but nothing is lost" I was after. Nailed it.

**3 — Undo.** Ticking the green circle to pop it back into the pile — yes, that safety net absolutely matters to me. I'll misfire and tick the wrong one, or realize I'm not actually done. Knowing I can just un-check it without hunting through menus means I'll trust the whole gesture. Keep it.

**4 — Getting things in.** Both ways work and both feel natural — the checkbox at save time for when I *know* I'm stashing to read, and the little **To read** button on a link later for when I change my mind. Good to have both.

On your assumptions:

- **The check-off gesture** — the circle right on the row is perfect. Immediate, no menu, no digging into Edit. Don't move it. Marking something read is a quick reflexive "done!" — it should live right where I'm looking.
- **Keeping ✓ Read visible** — yes, keep it. Hiding it would make a read link look identical to one I never touched, and I like *seeing* that I've been through it. "Done but kept" showing on the face of it is reassuring.
- **The big one — should saving default into to-read?** Here's my honest call: **no, keep it starting unticked, the way you have it.** I know I said a lot of my links come in wanting-to-read — and that's true — but not *all* of them. Sometimes I'm just filing a recipe I'm about to cook, or a reference I'll want later. If *everything* auto-landed in to-read, that pile would basically become "everything I've ever saved," and it'd lose all its meaning — the whole point is watching it *shrink* to zero, and that only works if it's things I actually mean to read. A pile I can never empty is just stressful.

  But — one thing that would honor what I said: **remember my last choice.** If I tick that box, keep it ticked for my next save, and if I untick it, leave it unticked. That way when I hit a stretch of stashing reading material, I tick it once and it stays; when I'm just filing, I untick once and it stays. It adapts to me instead of forcing one rule. That's the best of both.

This rounds out all four of my original promises, and honestly they all feel good. Really pleased with where this landed.

That's the best of both.

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously

Try these, in order:

**1 — The very first moment (empty state).** Before you touch anything, notice what an empty app says to you — the "Nothing saved yet 📎 / paste your first link" panel. Tell me if that feels welcoming and obvious for day one, or bleaves you unsure what to do.

**2 — The important one: a page it can't read.** Tick the dashed **"Simulate rough weather"** box, then paste any link and Save. Watch carefully. Tell me if what it does protects you — and whether it matches what you'd *want* to happen.

**3 — Compare.** Untick the box and save a normal link, so you can feel the difference between "read fine" and "couldn't read."

**4 — Gibberish.** Type something that isn't a link at all — like `asdf` — and hit Save. Tell me if how it responds feels right.

Here's what I decided, and where I most want your gut:

- **When it can't read the page, I chose to save it anyway** — with the web address standing in as the title, a clear "⚠️ couldn't read this — give it a name" flag, and a **Name it** button. My reasoning: the cardinal sin would be *losing* your link because a site was momentarily grumpy. Better to keep it and let you fix the name. But tell me — is "keep it, flag it, let me name it" right? Or would you rather it *tried again*, or refused to save until it worked?
- **Bad input gets a gentle inline nudge**, not a jarring popup — the box goes pink with a one-line explanation. Right touch, or too quiet?
- **The empty-state wording** — I wrote you a friendly first-run message; say if it should be warmer, plainer, or different.

And one honest gap I noticed while stress-testing that I should just ask you about plainly: **we've never talked about getting *rid* of a link.** When something's stale or you saved it by mistake — do you picture deleting it outright, and should a deleted link be truly gone, or recoverable in case you slip? No prototype yet — I just don't want to discover that hole later.

content:
Good round — this is the kind of "what happens when things go wrong" stuff I wouldn't have thought to ask for, but it matters.

**1 — Empty state.** Welcoming and obvious. "Nothing saved yet, paste your first link" told me exactly what to do on a blank screen, and the little note that the title and summary fill themselves in is a nice reassurance up front. No confusion. Good day-one feeling.

**2 — The page it couldn't read.** This is exactly right, and it's the single most important call you've made all along: **keep it, flag it, let me name it.** Please don't change that. The one thing that would break my trust completely is pasting a link, walking away thinking it's safe, and finding out it silently vanished because a site hiccupped. Saving it with the address standing in, the clear ⚠️ flag, and a "Name it" button means my link is *never* lost — worst case I do a little tidying. That's the whole promise honored even on a bad day. (Trying again once quietly in the background before giving up would be a fine bonus — but if it still fails, *keep it*. Never refuse to save.)

**3 — The comparison** made the difference obvious — clean fill-in versus the flagged one. Clear.

**4 — Gibberish.** The gentle pink nudge with a plain one-line explanation is the right touch. A big alarming popup for a simple typo would feel like being scolded. This just quietly points and lets me fix it. Keep it that quiet.

Empty-state wording is fine as-is — friendly without being cutesy.

Now — the two honest gaps, because you asked plainly:

**On a page that goes bad for good.** Your "dead link" test poked at a worry I hadn't put words to. Right now if I save something and the page later *disappears entirely* — taken down, site gone — all I've got is a dead address that opens nothing. For links I really cared about, that's still losing the thing, just slowly. So I'll put the question to you: is there any way that what I saved keeps a bit of *the page itself*, not just a pointer to it — so if the original ever vanishes, I've still got something to look at? I don't know how hard that is, but "the link still works a year later even if the site died" is squarely part of "I trust I won't lose it" for me.

**On getting rid of a link — yes, and it's actually two different feelings:**

- Sometimes a link is genuine junk — I saved it by mistake, or it's a typo. That one I want to **delete outright, gone.** But — and you know me by now — I'm the nervous type, so a delete shouldn't be a hair-trigger. Give me a small "are you sure," or better, a brief "deleted — undo?" moment. A single misclick shouldn't permanently cost me something.

- But there's a second, softer case I care about just as much: a link that *isn't* junk — I'm just **done** with it, or it's cluttering my main list — and I don't want to throw it in the trash, I want to **tuck it away out of sight but keep it safe**, in case someday I need it again. That's not deleting. That's more like "file it away in the back room." I'd want those tucked-away links *out* of my normal list and search so they're not in my face, but still somewhere I can go dig them back out and un-tuck them.

So really: **delete = gone for good (with a small safety beat), and a separate "put it away" = hidden but recoverable.** Those are two different needs in my head, and I'd hate for them to be the same button. Glad you flagged the hole before we hit it.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [7]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

A note first: on this screen the **Save** button is parked (saving's already settled on the earlier screens) — here we're only exercising delete and put-away. There's a link already sitting in the Put-away room so you can see how that looks.

**1 — Delete (the "this was a mistake" case).** Click **Edit** on a link, then the red **🗑 Delete…** on the right. It vanishes — but a bar slides up at the bottom offering **Undo**. Click Undo and confirm it comes right back, exactly where it was. Then delete one and *don't* undo, to feel that it's really gone. Tell me: does that undo moment give you enough of a safety beat, or would you want a proper "are you sure?" *before* it disappears instead?

**2 — Put away (the "I'm done, tuck it safe" case).** Edit a different link and click **🗄 Put away**. Watch it leave your main list. Now confirm it's truly *out of your face*: search for a word that's in it, and click through its old label — it shouldn't show up in either. Then click **🗄 Put away** at the top-right to visit the back room, find it there, and **↩ Put back**. Tell me if that "hidden but safe, and I can always dig it back out" feeling is what you meant.

Assumptions I want your read on:
- **Delete safety = an Undo moment**, not a blocking "are you sure?" — fewer nags, and one misclick never costs you anything as long as you glance at the bar. But you're the nervous type, so if you'd genuinely rather be *asked first*, say so and I'll switch it.
- **Put-away lives in the same Edit panel as Delete**, but clearly separated (quiet grey vs. red, opposite sides) so they're never confused for each other.
- **The back room is one click away** (top-right), with its own count — not buried.

---

And your question back to me — **can a saved link keep a piece of the page itself, so it survives even if the site later dies?** Honest answer: yes, that's absolutely doable — the app can keep its own snapshot of the page at the moment you save it, so even if the original vanishes, you've still got the text (and often the images) to look at. It's a real, well-trodden capability.

The only reason I'm not just folding it in silently: it's a **meatier piece** than the rest — it changes how much we store and adds a "here's the saved copy" view. So it's genuinely your call on *timing*, and I want to put it to you plainly:

- **Include it in this first build** — accepting that the first version takes a bit longer to reach your hands, but "the link still works a year later" is baked in from day one; or
- **Build the core you've shaped now, and add the snapshot as the very next thing** — you get everything we've designed sooner, with page-preservation as a fast follow.

Either is fine by me. Which sits better with you?

content:
This nailed both, and I'm glad they feel like the two separate things they are in my head.

**1 — Delete.** I edited a link, hit the red 🗑, it vanished, and the **Undo** bar slid up — clicked it and it came right back where it was. Then I deleted one and left it, and yes, that one's genuinely gone. Honest answer on your question: **the Undo moment is enough for me, and I actually prefer it to being asked "are you sure?" every time** — being nagged on every delete would get old fast, and this way one glance saves me. So keep the Undo approach.

One small thing, because I *am* the nervous type: make sure that Undo bar **lingers long enough that I actually notice it** — a few seconds, not a blink. My worry isn't the misclick I catch; it's the one where the bar vanishes before I realize what I did. As long as it sits there a comfortable beat, I'm happy. (And it being permanent *after* that is fine — that's what delete should mean. The "keep it safe" case is what Put away is for.)

**2 — Put away.** This is exactly what I meant. I tucked a link away, watched it leave my main list, then went hunting — searched a word that's in it, clicked through its old label — and it stayed properly out of sight in both. *Then* I popped open the Put-away room top-right, found it sitting there safe, and put it back. That "out of my face but never thrown out, and I can always dig it back out" feeling is precisely the middle ground I was after. The quiet grey versus the red, on opposite sides, means I'd never mix up "tuck away" with "destroy." And the back room being one click with its own count means I won't forget it exists. Really well done.

**On the snapshot — my call on timing:** **build the core we've shaped now, and make the snapshot the very next thing.** I'd rather get everything we've designed into my hands and start actually living in it, than wait longer up front. But I want to be clear this isn't a "someday, maybe" — page-preservation is genuinely important to me, so I'm counting on it as the *immediate* fast-follow, not something that quietly slips down a list. Firm next thing.

And one heads-up for when you build it, because it'll trip us up otherwise: **a real chunk of what I save isn't web pages at all — it's PDFs.** Reports, recipes people send me, articles saved as PDFs. When you're keeping a copy of the page so it survives, I'd want those PDFs kept too — the actual document, not just a snapshot of some wrapper around it. So whatever "keep a piece of it" ends up meaning, please make sure it does the sensible thing for a PDF and hangs onto the file itself. Just don't want that discovered late.

This has been a really solid stretch — delete and put-away both feel right. Happy to move on.

For a link that is genuine junk (mistake, typo), the client can delete it outright from the
manage area of the Edit panel (a red "🗑 Delete…", set apart on the opposite side from the
quiet "Put away"). The link disappears immediately and an Undo bar slides up at the bottom.

The client explicitly preferred this Undo moment over a blocking "are you sure?" on every
delete ("being nagged on every delete would get old fast"). Firm requirement: the Undo bar
must LINGER long enough to actually be noticed — a comfortable few seconds, not a blink —
because the dangerous case is the accidental delete the client hasn't yet realised they
made.

    Then the link is permanently removed

- Undo window is a few seconds (comfortably noticeable); permanence after that is intended.
- Delete is distinct in placement and colour from "Put away" so the two are never confused.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [10]

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)

  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"

- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

Here's where we've arrived. Over this stretch we've settled **twelve** flows, and honestly, they cover your whole original wish and then some. In plain terms, the app we've shaped together does this:

**The everyday core**
- **Paste a link, it sorts itself out** — fills in a readable title and summary so your list reads like real things, newest on top.
- **Open any link up to fix it** — a safe editing spot (Cancel/Esc always backs you out) for the title, the summary, and its labels.
- **Labels, not folders** — a link wears as many as you like, and typing one offers what you already have so you never breed "recipe" vs "recipes." Click a label to pull up that pile.
- **Search that finds the half-remembered** — type any words in any order, they all narrow it down; quotes mean exact. Reaches everything you can see on a link.
- **A "read later" pile** — a *state*, not a label; check things off and watch the pile shrink to zero, nothing lost.

**The trust safeguards**
- **Never a duplicate** — re-saving takes you to the one you have; tracking junk on a link is ignored, but genuinely different pages stay separate.
- **Never a lost link** — if a page can't be read, it's *still saved* and flagged for you to name; bad typos get a gentle nudge, not a scolding.
- **Two ways to let go** — **Delete** (gone for good, with an Undo beat) and **Put away** (hidden but safe in a back room you can always dig through).
- A friendly empty screen on day one.

**Firm next round (not this build):** keeping a snapshot of each page so links survive even if a site dies — including hanging onto PDFs as real files.

I think this scope is solid, complete, and genuinely yours — every piece came from your reactions, not my assumptions.

**May I switch over and start actually building this scope?** Once you say go, I'll move out of the shaping-and-prototyping mode we've been in and into building the real thing.

This is a genuinely lovely recap, and reading it back — yes, the heart of it is all there, and it feels like *mine*. I'm close to saying go. But you've earned my honesty by now, so let me do one careful gut-check before we cross over, because a couple of things I thought we'd landed aren't in your list, and one or two never quite got nailed down.

**Two things I asked for that I don't see in the recap:**

1. **A little note to myself on a link.** Way back when we built the edit panel I said I'd want to jot down *my own words* on a link — why I saved it, a reminder, "the bit halfway down is the good part." You even mentioned, when we did search, that you'd fold my notes into what search looks through "later." But your editing spot here only lists title, summary, and labels — my note seems to have quietly dropped out. I do want it. It doesn't need to be fancy — just a spot to write a few lines in my own voice.

2. **Remembering my "read later" default.** When we did the read-later pile, we agreed it'd *remember my last choice* — if I tick "add to read later" it stays ticked, if I untick it it stays off — so it adapts to whether I'm stashing reading or just filing. I don't see that in the summary; I want to make sure it didn't get lost.

**And a few things we either only half-touched or that I'm realizing now, at the "is this everything?" moment:**

3. **Getting my existing bookmarks *in*.** This is the big one. Remember, the whole reason I started was that I've already got a mountain of links piled up in my browser. If the only way in is pasting them one at a time, I'll never actually move over — that's hours of work and I just won't do it. I'd need a way to bring the whole lot across in one go. We never talked about it, and it suddenly feels important before you build.

4. **Getting my stuff back *out*.** The flip side, and it's a trust thing: if I'm going to pour my whole collection into this, I'd hate to feel trapped in it. I'd want to know I can get my own list back out — take it with me — if I ever needed to. Even just knowing it's possible would let me commit fully.

5. **Sorting the list other ways.** Newest-on-top is the right *normal*, and I like it. But once in a while I'd want to flip it — see my oldest saves, or line everything up by name to hunt something down. Just the ability to change the order now and then.

**And the handful we deliberately parked** — I just want to hear they're still on the list, not forgotten: pulling up **two labels at once** ("work stuff *and* still-to-read"), being able to **search inside just the pile I'm looking at**, **renaming a label everywhere in one go**, and keeping that **label bar tidy when I've got loads of them**. I'm fine with those coming later — I just don't want them to evaporate.

None of this is me second-guessing the core — the core is *right*, and I'm genuinely happy with it. But the note and the "remember my choice" were things we actually decided, and getting my existing pile in-and-out feels like the difference between me really living in this or not.

So: sort out those two dropped bits, tell me getting my bookmarks in and out is in the plan (or an honest "that's cycle two as well"), and then **yes — go build it.** I'm ready.

**The note.** I clicked Edit, wrote myself "the mushroom variation halfway down is the good part — double the garlic," hit Done, and there it is — in that soft highlighted "MY NOTE" block, clearly *mine* and not the auto-summary. And to answer your assumption directly: **yes, show it right on the link, not tucked inside Edit.** The whole point of a note is that it's a message to future-me, and future-me needs to *see* it without going digging. Having it sit right there on the card is exactly right. (One tiny thing: if I ever write a really long note, don't let it swallow the whole list — show me the first bit and let me open it up. But for normal little notes, perfect.)

**Search finding my note.** Confirmed — I searched `mushroom`, which is nowhere but in that note, and it dug it right out and highlighted it. That closes the loop on "something I jotted down myself." Really happy — search now covers every way I'd come looking.

**Sort.** Flipped to Oldest, then A–Z, then back. That's exactly what I wanted: newest-first is the right everyday normal, and being able to flip it now and then — to find my oldest saves or line things up by name — is all I needed. Good.

And on your plan for getting in and out — **yes, that's the right call, and I appreciate you not waving it away.** One short round to shape it, same as everything else, then we cross over. That's exactly the honesty that's made this work.

So, where my pile actually lives and how I'd wish to hand it over:

- **Mostly it's in my web browser's bookmarks** — that messy bar and the folders behind it I mentioned at the very start. There's also a scatter of links I've texted or emailed myself and a graveyard of open tabs, but the *bulk*, the part that matters, is the browser.
- I know my browser has some "export your bookmarks" thing that coughs up a file. So how I'd *wish* it worked: I hand you that one file, press a button, and my whole pile just… arrives. One go. I don't want to touch them one at a time — if I have to, I won't do it, and you're right that the whole thing dies there.

And since we're shaping it, here's what I'd quietly expect to *not* be a mess when a big pile lands:

- **Keep the names I already gave them.** A lot of my bookmarks I've already titled sensibly over the years — don't throw that away and re-guess.
- **My browser folders should turn into labels if they can.** I've got folders like "recipes" and "work" in there already — it'd be wonderful if those came across *as* labels so my organizing isn't all thrown on the floor and I start from scratch.
- **Don't collapse all my history to "today."** If everything imports stamped with today's date, then "newest first" becomes meaningless and years of my saving order just vanish. If it can remember roughly *when* I actually saved each one, I'd love that kept.
- **Don't make duplicates.** If a handful of them are things I've already saved in here, it should notice — same as it does when I re-paste — not give me two of everything.
- And it's going to be a *lot* of links at once — hundreds, maybe more. It should take that in stride and not make me sit there babysitting it.

**On getting out:** keep it simple — I'd want it to hand me back a normal file of my collection, the same everyday kind of bookmarks file, so I could load it into a browser or somewhere else if I ever needed. The thing I'm buying with that is peace of mind: I'm not locked in, so I can pour everything in without that trapped feeling. That's really all export needs to be.

Build me the "bring them in" moment to react to, and let's finish this.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [12]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

Walk it like this:

**1 — See it handle volume.** Click **"Try it with a big sample (600 links)."** Before *anything* changes, you get a preview card — read it. It should tell you, in real numbers, exactly what it's about to do: how many of your own titles it's keeping, which folders are becoming labels, the span of dates it found, and how many duplicates it'll skip. Nothing has happened yet.

**2 — Bring them in.** Press the blue **"Bring in … links"** button. Watch it take the whole pile in one go (there's a progress bar, no babysitting), then land them all in your list — joining the 3 you already had, each tagged **imported**, folders now showing as labels.

**3 — Check the date promise.** Flip **Sort → Oldest first**. If your years of saving order survived, you'll see the oldest sample saves rise to the top — not everything mashed to "today."

**4 — Your real pile (optional but the real test).** If you've got a moment, export your actual bookmarks from your browser and feed the file to **"Choose my bookmarks file…"** — I parse the real thing, not a fake. See if *your* folders and titles come across intact.

**5 — Getting out.** Once your list is populated, click **"⬇ Export my collection."** It hands you back a normal bookmarks file — the everyday kind you could load straight into a browser. That's your "I'm not locked in" guarantee, made real.

The assumptions I want your gut on:

- **The preview-before-anything-happens step.** I deliberately put a "here's what I'll do — nothing's changed yet" pause between handing over the file and committing. For a pile you care about, I figured you'd want to *look before you leap*. Tell me if that reassurance is welcome, or if it's a step you'd rather skip and just have them fly in.
- **Folders → labels.** A bookmark's folder becomes a label on it. Tell me if that's the mapping you pictured. (If you have folders-inside-folders, say so — I'll want to get that right.)
- **Duplicates on import** use the *same* smart rule as when you paste — so the sample sneaks in your "Lemon pasta" with a tracking tag on it and it still gets recognized and skipped. Confirm that's what you'd want.
- **Export is a plain bookmarks file** — simple and portable, exactly as you asked. Say if you'd expect your labels or notes to ride along in it too, or if a plain link-and-title file is enough for peace of mind.

This is the last thing to shape. Get these feeling right, and we cross over.

content:
This is the one that makes or breaks whether I actually move over — and it mostly lands beautifully. Let me go through it.

**The preview-before-anything-happens step — yes, keep it, this is exactly right.** Handing over my whole pile is nerve-wracking, and that "here's what I'm about to do, nothing's changed yet" pause with real numbers is precisely the "look before I leap" reassurance I needed. Seeing it spell out "600 found, keeping your titles, these folders becoming labels, dates span this to that, skipping 2 duplicates" — before committing — completely settles me. Don't ever make it just fly them in silently.

**Volume, dates, duplicates — all confirmed.** I ran the 600 sample: it took the whole lot in one go with the progress bar, no babysitting. I flipped to Oldest-first and my years of order were there — oldest saves rose to the top, not everything mashed to today. That date promise mattered to me and it held. And it caught the sneaky duplicates (the Lemon pasta with the slash, the BBC one with the tracking tag) and skipped them, using the same smart rule as pasting — and kept *my* nicer title rather than the browser's. All good.

Now — three things I need to flag before we cross, and one of them is important:

1. **The important one: capital letters are going to split my piles.** I noticed after importing I'd have both a "work" label (from what I'd already saved) *and* a "Work" label (from the imported folder) — and "recipes" *and* "Recipes." Those are the *same pile* to me, just different capitalization, and now they're two! That's the exact mess I asked you to protect me from way back — the "recipe vs recipes" thing. So when my folders come in as labels, please match them against labels I already have *ignoring capitalization*, the same way it does when I type a label by hand. I should not walk out of an import with my collection split across "work" and "Work."

2. **Folders-inside-folders — yes, I've got those, and I don't want the outer one lost.** My browser has things like "Recipes → Italian" and "Work → Q3." Right now it looks like only the *innermost* folder becomes the label, so a link buried in "Recipes → Italian" would come in tagged just "Italian" and lose that it's even a recipe. I'd want *both* levels kept as labels — "recipes" *and* "italian" — so nothing about how I'd sorted it gets thrown away. Getting that right matters, since the whole point is my organizing survives the move.

3. **On export — plain link-and-title is *not* quite enough for me, actually.** The links surviving is good, but think about what I'd be walking out *without*: all the labeling and all the notes I've painstakingly built up in here. If export hands back bare links with no labels, then even though I'm "not locked in" on the links, my entire filing system *is* trapped — I'd have to rebuild it from scratch anywhere else. So please carry my **labels** along in that file too (as folders — that's how a bookmarks file holds them, and it'd drop me right back into a browser organized the way I had it). My **notes** riding along would be a lovely bonus if it's possible, but labels I'd really want. *That's* what real peace of mind looks like to me — I can leave with my links *and* the order I put them in.

Sort out the capital-letters merge and the nested folders, carry my labels into the export, and honestly — **that's it, I'm ready to cross over and have you build the real thing.** This has been a genuinely great way to work; I feel like what you're about to build is actually mine.

Scenario ID: SCN-015
Title: Bring in my existing bookmarks in one go
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
The client hands over the file their browser produces when it "exports bookmarks" (the
bulk of their pile lives in the browser). They press one button and the whole pile arrives
— no per-link work (the client was firm: if it's one-at-a-time, they won't do it and the
whole product fails for them).

A PREVIEW step comes first and is required: before anything changes, the app shows, in
real numbers, exactly what it will do — nothing is committed until the client presses the
button. The client called this look-before-you-leap pause essential for handing over a pile
they care about.

The import honours all of these, shown in the preview and then done:
1. Keep the titles the client already gave their bookmarks (don't re-guess them).
2. Turn folders into labels — and:
   - match against existing labels IGNORING capitalisation (a "Work" folder joins the
     existing "work" label; never a "Work"/"work" split). Same protection as typing a
     label by hand.
   - keep BOTH levels of nested folders ("Recipes → Italian" → both "recipes" and
     "italian"); the outer level is never lost.
   - do NOT turn browser container wrappers ("Bookmarks bar", "Bookmarks Menu", "Other
     Bookmarks", etc.) into labels.
3. Preserve each bookmark's original save date so "oldest first" stays meaningful; do not
   stamp everything "today".
4. Skip duplicates using the same smart rule as pasting (ignores tracking junk; keeps the
   existing copy and its nicer title). Also merges same-URL entries appearing under
   multiple folders into one link carrying multiple labels.
5. Take hundreds+ in stride, all at once, with progress shown and no babysitting.

## Gherkin
Feature: Importing existing bookmarks

  Scenario: Preview before committing
    Given I have chosen my exported bookmarks file
    When the app reads it
    Then it shows what it will do and changes nothing until I confirm

  Scenario: Folders become labels, capitals merged, nesting kept
    Given a bookmark in folder "Recipes → Italian" and an existing label "recipes"
    When I import
    Then the bookmark carries labels "recipes" and "italian"
    And no separate "Recipes" label is created

  Scenario: Container folders are not labels
    Given bookmarks under a "Bookmarks bar" wrapper
    When I import
    Then "Bookmarks bar" does not become a label

  Scenario: Dates preserved
    Given imported bookmarks with original save dates
    When I sort oldest-first
    Then the earliest originals appear first, not everything dated today

  Scenario: Duplicates skipped
    Given a bookmark that matches one already saved (even with tracking junk)
    When I import
    Then it is skipped and my existing copy and title are kept

## Assumptions
- Input is the standard browser bookmarks export (Netscape HTML). Other sources (texted/
  emailed links, open tabs) are out of scope for this flow; browser file is the bulk.

- SCN-002 (duplicate rule), SCN-004 (label reuse), SCN-014 (sort needs the dates), SCN-016 (export)

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [14]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

# Design-decision record — Bookmarks app (cycle 1)

Purpose: enough structure to (a) do impact analysis in later cycles and (b) regenerate
traditional design/test docs on request. Cycle 2's firm next item is page snapshots
(incl. keeping PDFs as real files) — the resolver/store seams below are where that lands.

## Interface form
A single-page web app opened in a browser on a laptop; no install. Data persists locally
(localStorage) so the client can just "pull it up." (Phone access = non-functional backlog.)

## Why this shape
- **Pure logic modules, DOM-free** (`js/model, labels, search, sort, importer, exporter,
  library`) — so the trust-critical rules (dedup, label case-merge, multi-word search,
  import mapping) are unit-tested independently of the UI. This is where correctness lives.
- **Browser-only modules** (`js/resolver`, `js/store`, `js/app`) — page-reading, persistence,
  and rendering. Isolated so the pure rules never depend on the environment.
- **`id = normalized URL`.** Dedup (SCN-002) is then structural: the same page can't occupy
  two ids. Normalisation drops `www.`, trailing slash, and tracking params; keeps
  page-selecting params. Used identically by paste-save and import.

## Key decisions & dropped alternatives
- **Title reading via `resolver.js` with graceful fallback (SCN-008).** Client-side `fetch`
  of arbitrary pages is often CORS-blocked; rather than depend on a backend now, the resolver
  tries best-effort and, on ANY failure, saves the link anyway with the address as a
  stand-in title + `needsName` flag. One quiet retry, then keep. A metadata proxy can be
  slotted in later behind the same interface. Dropped: mandatory backend (heavier; delays
  delivery) — deferred with snapshots to cycle 2.
- **Labels canonicalised case-insensitively** (`labels.js`). First-seen spelling wins; later
  variants (typed OR imported folders) reuse it. Kills "work"/"Work" and "recipe"/"recipes"
  splits (SCN-004, SCN-015). Dropped: forcing lowercase (loses the client's chosen casing).
- **Delete = remove + Undo toast; Put away = archived flag** (SCN-011/012). Two different
  intents, never the same control. Archived items are excluded from list, search, label
  piles, to-read — only visible in the "Put away" view.
- **Import shows a preview and commits nothing until confirmed** (SCN-015). Netscape parser
  is hand-rolled (no DOMParser) so it's testable in Node; container folders ("Bookmarks
  bar" etc.) are excluded from labels; nested folders yield BOTH levels; original ADD_DATE
  preserved for meaningful sort.
- **Export writes labels as folders + notes as `<DD>`** (SCN-016) so filing survives a move;
  round-trips back through import.
- **Search haystack = title + summary + site + note; multi-word = AND, quotes = phrase**
  (SCN-006, SCN-013). Highlighter returns segments (DOM-free) for testability.

## Data model (one bookmark)
`{ id, url, host, title, summary, note, labels[], toRead, read, archived, savedAt, needsName }`

## Files
- `js/model.js` normalisation, url parsing, fallback title
- `js/labels.js` case-insensitive label index
- `js/search.js` tokenize / matches / highlight-segments
- `js/sort.js` newest | oldest | a–z
- `js/library.js` pure ops: find-duplicate, visible-items(view)
- `js/importer.js` parse bookmarks HTML, plan import
- `js/exporter.js` build bookmarks HTML
- `js/resolver.js` (browser) page metadata + fallback
- `js/store.js` (browser) localStorage persistence + state ops
- `js/app.js` (browser) UI
- `tests/` node test harness over the pure modules

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 2]
- Current step: [Development — design and implementation]
- Approved scenarios: [16]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

The real thing is built and ready for you to accept. It's the actual app now — your data saved locally in your browser, everything wired to the tested logic — not a prototype.

**To open it**, run this from the project, then visit the address it prints:

```
cd implementation && python3 -m http.server 8000
```

Then open **http://localhost:8000** in your laptop browser. (It needs to be *served*, not opened as a file, so the pieces can load.)

Now let me guide you through confirming each thing we shaped — same as always, one action at a time. Please try each and tell me it behaves the way you approved:

**The everyday core**
1. **Paste & save** — drop in a real link. Watch the brief "figuring out…" then it fill in a title/summary, newest at the top. *(Honest note: to read the page it asks a helper service to fetch it; if that's blocked or you're offline, you'll see #6 instead — which is the point.)*
2. **Fix it** — click **Edit**, change the title, add a **note** in your own words, press **Done**. Then Edit again and press **Cancel** / **Esc** — confirm it backs out clean.
3. **Labels** — in Edit, add two labels to one link; type a partial one and confirm it offers an existing label to reuse (try a capitalized version of one you have — it should merge, not split). Click a label chip to pull up that pile.
4. **Search** — type two words that live apart in a link; confirm both light up. Search a word that's only in a **note**. Try `"quoted"` for exact.
5. **Read later** — tick "add to to-read" and save; open **📖 To read**; tick the circle to check one off and watch it leave the pile; find it still saved wearing **✓ Read**; tick again to undo.

**The safeguards**
6. **Never lost** — paste a made-up dead link (e.g. `https://nope.invalid/xyz`); confirm it's *still saved*, flagged "give it a name," never dropped.
7. **No duplicate** — save a link, save it again → it takes you to the one you have.
8. **Gibberish** — type `asdf`, Save → gentle pink nudge, no popup.
9. **Delete vs Put away** — in Edit, try **🗑 Delete** (then **Undo** in the bar) and **🗄 Put away** (then find it in the Put-away room and put it back).
10. **Sort** — flip Newest / Oldest / A–Z.

**Moving in & out**
11. **Import** — click **⬆ Import**, feed it your real browser bookmarks export; read the preview, bring them in, confirm your titles/folders/dates survived and duplicates were skipped.
12. **Export** — **⬇ Export**, and (the proof) feed that file back into Import to see your labels return as folders and notes ride along.

**Does the behaviour of all of these match what you approved?** If anything's off, tell me which — I'll classify it as either an implementation fix (back to building) or a scenario we need to correct, and sort it within this cycle. If it all holds up, give me your acceptance and I'll close out cycle one — with page snapshots + PDF-keeping teed up as the firm next cycle.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)

  - Goal statement: context/goals.md

  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration
